newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar - China mill awaits verdict on imports.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar - China mill awaits verdict on imports.

text.p: A south China sugar mill in Jiangmen has run into difficulties with the authorities over the documentation for a 14,000-tonne shipment of raw sugar from Thailand, Asian traders said on Wednesday.
They said the consignment lacked the requisite import licences. An official at the mill, asked by Reuters if this was the case, declined to comment on details.
"This matter is still being explored and there will be a decision," he said without elaboration. The official did not say when a decision on the cargo would be reached.
"The sugar was unloaded at Taishan and then transported in small barges to Jiangmen since the mill is not by the sea," one sugar source said.
Traders said last week that a 14,000-tonne cargo of Thai sugar was discharging at the southern Chinese port of Taishan, but whether the buyer had a valid import or tolling licence was questionable.
The problems faced by Jiangmen's sugar mill made the fate of two other cargoes headed for China very uncertain, they added.

Traders said that the Marina Lauri, which left Thailand on March 7 carrying 10,000 tonnes of raw sugar in bags, had arrived at China's marine borders near Xingang port at the northern city of Tianjin.
"The ship is not berthed, and will be inspected," said a sugar trader, adding he expected the cargo would be the subject of negotiations between the Chinese government and the buyer.

"Up to now, not one tonne in import licences have been issued," a senior sugar source said, noting that China's sugar import market was highly sensitive to changes in supply so a lot of attention is focused on the imports.

China's domestic sugar prices have dipped slightly to about 3,950 yuan ($476) a tonne over the past week as stocks have grown, but sellers are confidently awaiting a recovery in the market by May, sources in the producing province of Guangxi said.

The Asian sugar market generally has been very quiet this week with little business done so far and Thai raw premiums slipping due to slack physical demand, Japanese traders said. They said the premiums were likely to ease further.
"Buyers are waiting for sugar premiums to ease more before they enter the market," one trader in Japan said.

Thai raw sugar premiums for May/July delivery were quoted weaker, at 0.20/0.35 cents per pound (bid/offer), against 0.25/0.40 cents a week earlier, over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on a FOB basis.
July/September deliveries were quoted at 0.50/0.65 cents, compared with 0.60/0.90 cents a week ago.
Market talk that China would not buy any sugar in the spot market this year is undermining sentiment, Japanese traders said. ($1=8.3 yuan)
